solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Knight has king in for wallop

indicators.note: with 'in', the knighting word has the king put inside it
with 'has', the king goes in the middle of the knighting word

parts.note: to dub someone is to knight them with a touch of the sword
R is short for Rex, Latin for king

explanation.surface: A knight with a king for company is about to deliver a heavy blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knight' looks like a noun but is the verb DUB, which 'has' R (Rex) 'in' it.
explanation.definitionFit: To drub is to beat soundly, a synonym of wallop as a verb.

clue.text: Graze by the sound of it in northern pastures

definitions.note: Chambers gives raik as a Scots word for pasture or range, used of grazing ground in general, hence the plural

indicators.note: tells us the scraping word is only heard, and a different spelling goes in the grid

parts.note: to rake is to scrape or graze a surface

explanation.surface: Cattle grazing on the hills of the north, as heard in a local accent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Graze' looks like the grazing of cattle, but here it means scratch, RAKE; 'by the sound of it' gives the Scots word that sounds the same. 'Northern' marks the answer as Scots.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots dialect a raik is a stretch of grazing land over which animals range.

clue.text: What commuter catches in the morning, leaning back (first off) having caught elevated railroad

definitions.text: What commuter catches in the morning

indicators.note: the shortened word takes the railway letter inside it
the first letter of the reclining word is dropped

parts.note: supine means lying or leaning on one's back
an elevated railroad in the US, as in Chicago, is called the L or El

explanation.surface: A commuter lounging back gets on an overhead railway train in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: With 'first off', SUPINE becomes UPINE, which, 'having caught' L, the American name for an overhead railway, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The up line is the railway track for trains heading to the capital, which commuters board each morning.

clue.text: Nasty Aussie insect turned up entirely in belly (7, two words)

indicators.note: the reversed word sits inside the sail word

parts.note: the bunt is the bellying middle part of a sail or fishing net

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned up means the whole-amount word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: all means entirely, as in 'all wrong'

explanation.surface: An unpleasant Australian bug crawls right up into someone's stomach.
explanation.walkthrough: 'belly' is a sailing term here: the bunt is the bellying middle of a sail or net. In a down entry 'turned up' reads the whole-amount word upwards as LLA, and 'in' puts it inside.
explanation.definitionFit: The bull ant is a large Australian ant with a fierce and painful sting.

clue.text: Strong drink? After school dozes, having imbibed pastis (not wines)

indicators.note: the school-and-dozing letters drink in, that is contain, what is left of the French drink

parts.note: SCH, the dictionary abbreviation for school, followed by NAPS, meaning dozes

indicators.note: the wines are taken away from the word pastis

parts.note: taken as written: the aniseed spirit
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine, so Astis are wines

explanation.surface: After lessons someone naps, having drunk pastis rather than wine; what they really want is something strong.
explanation.walkthrough: Asti is an Italian sparkling wine, so 'not wines' strips the plural of it from the aniseed spirit, leaving one letter; SCH and NAPS (dozes after school), 'having imbibed' it, give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Schnapps is a strong spirit, so it is a strong drink.

clue.text: Many pets love this — cover the top of round tin that's damaged

indicators.note: the capping word goes round the jumbled metal word

parts.note: to cap something is to cover its top

indicators.note: the word tin is damaged, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Instructions for sealing a battered round tin of something cats adore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'round tin' looks like a shape of tin, but 'round' is the containment signal, and 'that's damaged' scrambles the metal word into TNI.
explanation.definitionFit: Catnip is a plant whose scent many cats find irresistible.

clue.text: Former land-tax kept under wraps a long time

parts.note: an age is a very long time

explanation.surface: An old tax on land that was concealed for many years.
explanation.definitionFit: Hidage was a tax paid on each hide of land in Anglo-Saxon and Norman England.

clue.text: Tally about right, slightly off

indicators.note: the askew word goes about, that is around, the letter for right

parts.note: agee (also ajee) is Scots for off the straight, awry

explanation.surface: A count that is almost correct but a little wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: AGEE is a Scots word for askew; 'about' puts it around R.
explanation.definitionFit: To tally is to agree or correspond, as when two accounts match.

clue.text: Former idol, a divinity, put in personal appearance

indicators.note: the article and the deity are put inside the appearance abbreviation

explanation.surface: An old idol, a god, makes a public appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put in' places the god inside PA. Chambers records the answer as an old word for an idol.
explanation.definitionFit: Pagoda once also meant an idol or image of a god in an Eastern temple, a sense now obsolete.

clue.text: Mantle, eastern, in puckered fabric

indicators.note: the letter for eastern goes inside the fabric word

parts.note: plissé is a cloth with a puckered or pleated finish

explanation.surface: An Eastern cloak made from crinkled cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: A pelisse is a long cloak or fur-trimmed outer garment, a kind of mantle.

clue.text: Cover for pair of GIs in camp the rest lent out (11, two words)

definitions.text: Cover for pair of GIs in camp

indicators.note: out signals that these letters are put out of order

explanation.surface: Soldiers in camp share a cover, and everyone else's has been loaned out.
explanation.definitionFit: A shelter tent is a small two-man tent carried in halves by US soldiers.

clue.text: Nut tree, source of a cup Asia fashioned

indicators.note: the words are fashioned into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tree whose nut provides a drinking cup made in Asia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashioned' rearranges A CUP ASIA; 'source of' links the definition to the wordplay, teasingly hinting that the cup comes from the tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The sapucaia is a South American tree whose large woody pods hold edible paradise nuts.

clue.text: Flax-cutter's tool, form of wand English waved

indicators.note: the letters are waved about into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone waves a wand in the English way as if it were a tool for flax.
explanation.walkthrough: 'waved' rearranges WAND and ENGLISH together; 'form of' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A swingle-hand is the wooden blade used to scutch flax, beating the fibres free.

clue.text: Wader feeble, ailing internally

indicators.note: the sick word goes inside the feeble word

explanation.surface: A weak, sickly wading bird.
explanation.definitionFit: The willet is a large North American wading bird of the sandpiper family.

clue.text: Writer's hollow task, article for the French

parts.note: darg is a Scots and northern word for a day's work or task
le is the French masculine definite article

explanation.surface: An author's empty assignment is a piece written for French readers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Writer's' means the word is a particular author's: Chambers marks dargle as used by Sir Walter Scott.
explanation.definitionFit: A dargle is a wooded dell, a hollow, in Scott's usage.

clue.text: Almost bare in earth? Treatment with this is useless

indicators.note: the shortened word sits inside the earth word
the bare word loses its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone almost naked buried in mud, being told such a cure does no good.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the whole second sentence, a description rather than a synonym. 'Almost' trims the bare word to NAKE, and 'in' places it inside the earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Snake oil is a fake remedy, so any treatment with it is worthless.

clue.text: Number attached to England, wavering about independence, without agreeing

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase: not allied or in agreement with either side

indicators.note: the jumbled country goes about, that is around, the letter for independence
the letters of England waver into a new order

parts.note: I is a standard abbreviation for independent or independence

explanation.surface: A numbered team linked with England is unsure about independence, failing to agree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wavering' turns the country into NALGNED, which goes 'about' the I of independence to make NALIGNED; 'attached to' is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonaligned state is one that stays out of alliances, not siding with any bloc.

clue.text: That old-fashioned twinkle exhibited by man catching first sight of lass

indicators.note: the man word catches, that is contains, the lass's first letter
only the first letter of the girl word is seen

explanation.surface: A man spots a girl for the first time and shows a twinkle in his eye.
explanation.definitionFit: Glent is an obsolete form of glint, a flash or gleam of light.

clue.text: Bowling ball, over almost attracting affection

indicators.note: bowling suggests rolling the letters around into a new order
the word over is cut short by its last letter

explanation.surface: A cricket delivery in the last over draws warm applause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowling ball' looks like one object, but 'Bowling' is the anagram signal on BALL plus OVE, which is 'over' made 'almost'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something lovable easily draws fondness from others.

clue.text: Seek help with engraving

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to pursue or seek
second meaning: to ... metal is to decorate it by embossing or engraving

explanation.walkthrough: It reads as a request for assistance, but splits into two separate meanings of the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means both to pursue something and to work decoration into metal, as an engraver does.

clue.text: Trace rigidity without inner depth

indicators.note: the letter for depth is removed from inside the rigidity word

explanation.surface: Someone tries to find signs of stiffness lacking any real substance within.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trace' looks like a verb, but a trace is one of the straps of a horse's harness. 'without inner' drops D from the middle of the rigidity word.
explanation.definitionFit: Traces are the side straps by which a horse pulls a cart, so they are part of the tack.

clue.text: Set free once, so let out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are put out of their order

explanation.surface: Someone was released in the past, so they were let out.
explanation.definitionFit: Loste is a Spenserian past tense of loose, meaning released.

clue.text: Old helmet to recognize when lifted

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifted means the letters are read upwards

parts.note: to tell is to recognize or distinguish, as in 'tell them apart'
as means when, as in 'as he arrived'

explanation.surface: You can identify an old helmet when it is raised.
explanation.definitionFit: A sallet is a light rounded helmet of the fifteenth century.

clue.text: The lady's upset for this reason? No longer

parts.note: her means belonging to the lady
to eat someone is to upset or worry them, as in 'what's eating you?'

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether this is why the woman is distressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like an anagram signal, but it is EAT. 'No longer' marks the answer as archaic.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereat is an archaic adverb meaning at this, or because of this.

clue.text: 'Carry-on' woman with chaps endlessly is responsible for such a caper

parts.note: Carry On Cleo is a 1964 British comedy film about Cleopatra

indicators.note: the last letter of the chaps word is dropped

explanation.surface: A comedy-film heroine and her men are behind such a madcap prank.
explanation.walkthrough: Carry On films are a long-running series of British farce comedies; 'endlessly' trims MEN to ME. 'caper' looks like a prank but is the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Cleome is a genus of flowering plants in the caper family, so it is a kind of caper.

clue.text: Drum, one of a pair, is damaged? Could be ear skin

indicators.note: the answer and the word is, mixed up, make the words ear skin

parts.note: taken as written: the letters that the answer plus 'is' rearrange into

explanation.surface: A drum in a pair has a damaged skin, perhaps the eardrum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'damaged' says the answer plus IS, rearranged, gives EARSKIN.
explanation.definitionFit: A naker is a medieval kettledrum, played in pairs.

clue.text: A 'K' a Singh's deployed … is this?

definitions.text: A 'K' a Singh's deployed … is this?

indicators.note: the letters are deployed, set out afresh, so the answer plus 'is' rearranged gives the words

explanation.surface: A Sikh uses one of the five Ks: is this one of them?
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Singh's' as Singh is: 'deployed' says A K A SINGH is the answer plus IS, rearranged. Singh is the name taken by Sikh men.
explanation.definitionFit: The kangha is a wooden comb, one of the five Ks that baptised Sikhs keep.

clue.text: Earl unhappily admitted stress getting faster

definitions.note: used adjectivally: accelerant can describe something that speeds up

indicators.note: the stress word admits, that is contains, the jumbled nobleman

parts.note: an accent is a stress on a syllable

indicators.note: unhappily suggests the letters of Earl are out of sorts and rearranged

explanation.surface: An unhappy earl put under stress grows quicker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unhappily' scrambles the nobleman into LERA and 'admitted' puts it inside the stress word, an accent.
explanation.definitionFit: Accelerant means accelerating, speeding up, as well as being a substance that hastens a reaction.

clue.text: Call from a poet arrived with Latin in

indicators.note: the letter for Latin goes inside the arrival word

explanation.surface: A poet came along with some Latin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a poet' marks a Spenserian word; 'in' puts L inside the arrival word.
explanation.definitionFit: Clame is Spenser's spelling of claim, which once meant to call out.

clue.text: Whereon to park stetsons fixed there, the lot included? (8, two words)

indicators.note: the jumbled word includes the everything word
the word there is fixed, that is repaired into a new order

explanation.surface: Cowboy hats all hung up there, every one of them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fixed' looks like hung up, but scrambles the word there into HTREE, and 'included' puts the lot inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A hall tree is an American coat-and-hat stand, a place to hang Stetsons.

clue.text: What may accompany bill topping millions? It's grimy

indicators.note: in a down entry, the cooing word sits on top of the millions letter

parts.note: lovers bill and coo, so coo accompanies bill
M is the abbreviation for million

explanation.surface: Something that goes with a huge bill and is dirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bill' looks like money, encouraged by 'millions', but lovers bill and coo; 'topping' puts that word above M in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Coom is coal dust or grime, so it is a grimy substance.

clue.text: Surgically remove bit of lump to nullify circles

indicators.note: the nullifying word circles, that is surrounds, the first letter of lump

parts.note: to abate a nuisance or writ is to nullify it in law

indicators.note: only the first letter of the swelling word is taken

explanation.surface: A surgeon cuts away part of a lump to stop it spreading.
explanation.definitionFit: To ablate is to remove tissue surgically, by cutting or burning.

clue.text: State about to welcome European artist

indicators.note: the concerning word welcomes, that is takes in, the painter

parts.note: Paula Rego was a Portuguese-born painter

explanation.surface: A US state prepares to receive a visiting painter from Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'State about to' looks like a phrase, but 'about' is ON, and 'to welcome' takes in Paula Rego, the Portuguese painter.
explanation.definitionFit: Oregon is a state in the north-west United States.

clue.text: Depots currently fashionable offering protection for banks

parts.note: hot means in fashion right now

explanation.surface: Trendy depots that provide security for banks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' looks financial but means riverbanks.
explanation.definitionFit: Campshot is a facing of piles and boards protecting a riverbank from erosion.

clue.text: With tons etc crookedly caught in the act, spotted by the police?

indicators.note: the shuffled letters are caught in the act word
crookedly signals the letters are bent out of order

explanation.surface: A crook with tons of loot is caught red-handed by the police.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' is a link. 'crookedly' scrambles the tons letter with etc into TECT, and 'caught in' places it inside the act word, a deed; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: Something detected has been discovered or noticed, as crimes are by police.

clue.text: Title of distinguished Japanese book, short one

parts.note: Sam is the short form of Samuel, a book of the Bible

explanation.surface: A short book about a distinguished Japanese person's title.
explanation.definitionFit: Sama is a Japanese honorific added to names of people held in high esteem.
